text: ServiceNow separates configuration into two scopes that are easy to confuse if you've only ever clicked around casually. System settings apply instance-wide, to everyone, or to everyone holding a given role. Personal preferences apply only to the individual user who set them, and never touch anyone else's session.

System settings live behind the gear icon in the header, or more fully inside the System Properties application, which is typically restricted to users with administrative roles. Personal preferences live behind the user's own profile picture or user menu instead, and any logged-in user can open and change their own, regardless of what role they hold.

System Properties governs instance-wide behavior — default list page sizes, whether certain modules or features are turned on for the whole instance, session and security configuration, and countless other properties that change how the platform behaves for every single user who hits them. A careless change here doesn't just affect the person making it, which is exactly why it's gated behind an administrative role.

Personal preferences cover one user's own experience of the instance: date and time format, display time zone, language, notification preferences, theme, and list or form display settings such as how many rows show per page. Two agents sitting right next to each other can have completely different time zones, languages, and notification settings without either one's choice touching the other's session at all.

Mixing these up causes two real mistakes — hunting through System Properties to fix what was actually your own time zone or date format, or assuming something is personal when it's really instance-wide and changing it for everyone by accident. Knowing which scope you're in before you touch anything is a basic but genuinely load-bearing admin skill. Next up: a worked navigation lab putting everything from this chapter together.
